mcqs.question: Why is LRU a common default eviction policy, despite alternatives existing?
options: It needs no configuration and performs reasonably well across a wide range of access patterns due to temporal locality
It guarantees the highest possible hit ratio for every workload
It's the only eviction policy that can be implemented in O(1) time
It never evicts data that will be accessed again
mcqs.explanation: LRU's appeal is being a solid, zero-tuning default that fits many real workloads' recency bias. It doesn't guarantee the best hit ratio universally (LFU can beat it for stable long-term popularity), other policies like FIFO can also run in O(1), and no eviction policy can promise it never removes something needed again.

mcqs.question: A set of items has been consistently popular for months, but LRU keeps evicting one of them during short bursts of unrelated traffic. Which policy is better suited here?
options: FIFO, since it removes the oldest items regardless of usage
LFU, since it tracks total access frequency over time rather than only recency
LRU with a shorter TTL, since that fixes the eviction problem
No eviction policy — disable eviction entirely
mcqs.explanation: LFU tracks frequency over time, so a long-term popular item accumulates a high count that survives a brief quiet period, unlike LRU which only looks at the most recent access. FIFO ignores usage entirely and would evict just as poorly. A shorter TTL addresses freshness, not eviction choice, and disabling eviction isn't viable under bounded memory.

mcqs.question: A cache entry can be removed even when there's plenty of free memory available. Why?
options: TTL expiry removes entries once they're no longer considered fresh, independent of memory pressure
This should never happen — removal only occurs when the cache is full
The cache is malfunctioning if this occurs
Eviction policies always run on a fixed timer regardless of TTL
mcqs.explanation: TTL is about correctness/freshness, not capacity — an entry can expire and be removed the moment its TTL passes, whether or not memory is full. Eviction policies (LRU/LFU/FIFO) are the ones tied to capacity pressure; TTL is a separate, independent mechanism, not a malfunction or a fixed-timer eviction rule.

mcqs.question: In the hashmap + doubly linked list LRU implementation, what makes both get and put run in O(1)?
options: The cache periodically re-sorts the entire linked list by recency in the background
It scans the whole list on every operation but the list is kept very short
It uses a separate timestamp field and sorts by timestamp on each access
The hashmap gives direct node lookup and the linked list allows moving/removing any node with a constant number of pointer updates
mcqs.explanation: O(1) comes from combining a hashmap (instant node lookup by key) with a doubly linked list (constant-time unlink/re-link of any node, since each node knows its neighbors). There's no background re-sort, no full-list scan, and no per-access sort by timestamp — those would all cost more than O(1).

mcqs.question: A nightly batch job sequentially reads every row of a large table exactly once through an LRU cache. What's the likely effect?
options: The scan evicts the genuinely hot working set, replacing it with data unlikely to be reused
No effect — LRU only evicts data that's never been accessed
The cache automatically detects the scan and ignores it for recency tracking
Hit ratio improves, since the cache now holds more total data
mcqs.explanation: Because the scan touches every key once, LRU marks all of them as recently used, which can flush out the small set of genuinely hot keys the application relies on day to day — a classic LRU thrashing scenario. Plain LRU has no built-in scan detection, and hit ratio typically drops afterward, not improves, since the working set was replaced with rarely-reused data.
